newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Veteran foe says Mobutu named him as new Zaire PM.
newsitem.headline: Veteran foe says Mobutu named him as new Zaire PM.

text.p: Zaire's radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi said in a radio interview on Friday that his arch foe President Mobutu Sese Seko had given him a mandate to form a national unity government.

Tshisekedi told Radio France International after talks late on Thursday with Mobutu, who is in southern France recuperating from cancer surgery, that dialogue was the only way to end a revolt by Tutsi and other Mobutu opponents in the east.

"It must be resolved through negotiation because we have already shed too much blood of our people," he said, playing down the role of neighbouring Rwanda and adding that the month-old revolt was essentially an internal problem.

Tshisekedi's supporters among students in Kinshasa have been at the forefront of a campaign against part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and spearheading demands that the army be given the means to impose a military solution.

Tshisekedi said rebel leader Laurent Kabila, another veteran Mobutu foe, should have a role in Zaire as he too was party to the decisions of a 1992 sovereign national conference which Mobutu had re-endorsed.

The conference, which effectively launched Zaire's much-delayed democratic transition, elected Tshisekedi prime minister but Mobutu shunted him aside in 1993, a decision Tshisekedi has always refused to accept.
"With this reconciliation that we have just had, President Mobutu... will respect the constitutional act so that I lead what we call a government of national unity," he said.

"Kabila is a son of the country... having a stake in this project (of the national conference) he should be able to find what he needs in it because it is a problem concerning the Zairean family," he added.

"I have done what is necessary -- reconciliation between the two political families," he said, adding that he visited Mobutu in the national interest. "We will form a national unity government which will attack these problems in the east."
Kabila's rebels hold a string of major towns and territory along the border with Rwanda and Burundi. Kengo's government has repeatedly accused Rwanda's Tutsi-led army of invading.
